characters: Abena: 11-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat braided hair, wearing a crisp school uniform and carrying her science detective notebook.
Nana Yaw: Abena’s lively 9-year-old younger brother in a blue striped shirt, curious and expressive.
Madam Lamptey: Knowledgeable Primary 6 science teacher wearing a green kaba-and-slit outfit and glasses.
Mother: Caring Ghanaian mother in a warm patterned dress.

narrationPlan.voice: Expressive, clear Ghanaian-English storyteller voice (Kore) with playful sibling banter and precise scientific explanation
narrationPlan.pace: Steady fluent-reader pace (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Emphasize the rule to seek professional clinic testing for fever rather than self-diagnosing.

music: Curious Detective Marimba & Piano (light, inquisitive piano melody ducked beneath narration)
culturalNotes: Insecticide-treated bed nets, compound sanitation and clinic malaria testing (RDT/microscopy) are key public-health practices across Ghana.
Abena (Tuesday-born girl) and Nana Yaw (Thursday-born boy) are classic Akan names; Lamptey is a Ga family name.
reviewQuestions: Does the story clearly distinguish between the Plasmodium parasite (the cause of malaria) and the infected female Anopheles mosquito (the vector)?
Does the story emphasize professional clinic testing for fever and avoid any instruction to self-diagnose or self-medicate?

pages.brief: 3D animated bright Ghanaian bedroom morning scene. Young Nana Yaw sits on his bed holding his blanket with a grumpy expression while his older sister Abena in her school uniform holds a science notebook and smiles encouragingly.
pages.narration: Open with a playful mosquito buzz, grumpy humour for Nana Yaw, and bright confidence for Abena.

pages.brief: 3D animated Ghanaian science classroom. Madam Lamptey in a green patterned dress points to an educational illustration of a mosquito and microscopic parasites on a board while Abena writes in her detective notebook and Nana Yaw listens intently.
pages.narration: Clear, careful pronunciation of "Plasmodium" and "Anopheles", emphasizing the distinction between parasite and carrier.

pages.brief: 3D animated outdoor school compound scene in Ghana. Madam Lamptey supervises Abena, Nana Yaw and classmates at a safe distance from an uncovered plastic bucket holding rainwater, while the school caretaker approaches to empty and cover it safely.
pages.narration: Curious detective tone on the compound walk, with clear emphasis on reporting standing water to adults.

pages.brief: 3D animated clean Ghanaian community clinic. Nana Yaw sits beside his mother while a friendly Ghanaian health worker in a clinical coat explains a diagnostic test with a reassuring smile.
pages.narration: Warm, reassuring tone from Mother and the health worker explaining why testing is essential before diagnosis.

pages.brief: 3D animated Ghanaian home bedroom scene. Mother, Abena and recovered Nana Yaw carefully inspect a clean white insecticide-treated mosquito net and tuck it neatly around the mattress near a screened window.
pages.narration: Calm, practical family discussion showing layered malaria prevention.

pages.brief: 3D animated Ghanaian classroom scene. Abena stands at the front holding her detective notebook and explaining malaria transmission while Madam Lamptey nods approvingly and Nana Yaw raises his hand.
pages.narration: Clear, articulate delivery highlighting the scientific distinction between standing water, mosquito vectors and parasites.

pages.brief: 3D animated lively school science fair in Ghana. Abena and Nana Yaw stand proudly beside a colourful paper craft model of the mosquito life cycle and transmission diagrams while visiting parents and teachers admire the displays.
pages.narration: Proud, upbeat atmosphere at the school science exhibition.

pages.brief: 3D animated cosy evening study scene at home. Abena sits at a wooden desk closing her notebook while Nana Yaw leans over her shoulder grinning, and both siblings laugh warmly together.
pages.narration: Read the case summary crisply like a detective’s report, ending with warm sibling laughter.

teacherGuide.overview: Do not collect or breed live mosquitoes for classroom activities. Use photographs, diagrams and supervised environmental observations. Avoid giving children instructions to self-diagnose or self-medicate. Medical guidance should be reviewed against current Ghana Health Service and WHO recommendations before publication.
learningGoals: Distinguish between the organism that causes malaria (Plasmodium parasite) and the vector that transmits it (infected female Anopheles mosquito).
Explain why standing water supports mosquito development and how insecticide-treated bed nets, window screens and adult-managed sanitation reduce risk.
Explain why fevers require assessment and testing by a qualified health professional rather than self-diagnosis.

beforeReading: Ask learners what they know about mosquitoes and how families protect themselves from mosquito bites at night.
whileReading: Pause at Page 2 for the quick question on what causes malaria, reinforcing the difference between the Plasmodium parasite and the mosquito vector.
On Page 4, discuss why Nana Yaw’s mother took him to the clinic for testing instead of guessing.
afterReading: Complete the five end-of-story activities covering the Plasmodium parasite, infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, why not every fever is malaria, prevention measures, and the importance of diagnostic testing.
discussion: Why did Abena say that malaria is not caused by dirty water itself, even though standing water matters?
Why is it important never to self-diagnose or take medicine without a health professional’s advice?
reflection: What safe steps can your household take this week to check bed nets and report uncovered water containers to adults?

mathsExtension.task: If a community clinic tests 40 patients who have a fever and 25 test positive for malaria while 15 have other causes of fever, what fraction of the fever patients did NOT have malaria?
mathsExtension.answer: 15 out of 40 patients (or 3/8), showing why testing is essential before treatment.

support: Draw a simple 3-box chain on the board: Plasmodium parasite → Infected female Anopheles mosquito → Transmission to human.
stretch: Create a four-stage diagram of the mosquito life cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult) using paper and coloured pencils.

culturalNotes: Ghana Health Service and community clinics emphasize testing before treatment ("Test, Treat, Track") and sleeping under insecticide-treated nets.
localiseThis: Remind learners to report any uncovered water containers or blocked drains at school to the school caretaker or teachers rather than handling stagnant water themselves.

whatWeKnow: Human malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
Insecticide-treated bed nets, vector management and prompt professional testing and treatment reduce malaria illness.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Scientists continue researching more effective malaria vaccines, new antimalarial medicines and ways to overcome insecticide resistance.

investigation.title: Paper Model of the Mosquito Life Cycle & Prevention Poster
materials: Published reference diagrams of the mosquito life cycle
steps: Draw the four stages of the mosquito life cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult) on a poster using textbook diagrams.
Mark which stages live in standing water and how adult-managed covering or draining of containers interrupts breeding.
Add a clear reminder box: "Always visit a clinic for a malaria test when someone has a fever."
investigation.whatToNotice: Interrupting breeding sites and using treated bed nets reduce bites, while clinic testing ensures accurate diagnosis.
investigation.safetyNote: Do NOT collect, keep or breed live mosquitoes or larvae, and do not touch stagnant water.

factCheck.claim: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes; fevers require diagnostic testing.
factCheck.explanation: WHO and Ghana Health Service guidelines require parasitological confirmation (by RDT or microscopy) of suspected malaria before treatment.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (WHO) World Malaria Report & Ghana Health Service Malaria Case Management Guidelines
